description:
Vestige is a team of five students united by one idea: nothing left behind is ever truly gone. 

 For the 2026 challenge, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," we will turn NASA's open data into an experience that records where these objects are, what they did and why they matter. We bring together engineering, design and storytelling, so the past of space exploration can inspire the next frontier
summary:
What happens to the machines that take humanity beyond Earth after their missions are over? Do they simply become forgotten pieces of hardware? We think their stories deserve better.

Project Vestige is an interactive digital archive developed in response to the challenge of telling the stories of NASA's discarded and abandoned equipment on the Moon and Mars. It explores the machines, missions and scientific contributions that often receive less attention than the astronauts and discoveries they made possible.

Using NASA's open data, mission records and imagery, we transform scattered technical information into accessible, engaging stories of exploration, engineering, endurance and discovery.

The website brings this experience together through five key sections: Home, which introduces the project; Library, where visitors can explore selected equipment; Science, which provides scientific context; Story Pages, which bring individual machines and their journeys to life; and an interactive Quiz, which makes learning more engaging.

Our collection includes equipment from the Moon and Mars, alongside selected deep-space missions that extend the story of human exploration.

Why does this matter? Because preserving these stories helps us understand the history of space exploration, appreciate the engineering behind it, and make scientific knowledge more accessible to everyone.

With Project Vestige, the mission may be over, but the story isn't.
details: The website is designed around five interconnected sections: - Home: Provides an introduction and guides visitors into the experience. - Library: Serves as the main collection, allowing users to browse and explore the selected space equipment. - Story Pages: Take visitors beyond technical specifications, presenting each machine's origins, mission, journey, challenges and legacy through storytelling. - Science: Explores the scientific discoveries and engineering contributions associated with the equipment. - Quiz: Provides an interactive learning experience where visitors can test what they have discovered. How it works Visitors can navigate the website, select equipment from the library, explore individual stories, learn about the science behind the missions and reinforce their knowledge through the quiz. This creates a learning experience that combines exploration, storytelling and interaction. What makes it creative Our approach is to make machines the storytellers of human exploration. We use narrative, visual presentation and interactive elements to turn information that might otherwise feel technical or distant into something people can connect with. Rather than treating every piece of equipment as another historical record, we explore the different journeys and legacies behind them. Tools and technology The website was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Claude Artifacts supported some of the initial development, GitHub was used for code hosting and version management, and GitHub Pages was used to deploy and publish the website. We also incorporated NASA imagery and publicly available mission information as research resources. Benefits and intended impact Vestige provides an accessible way to explore space exploration history, encourages interest in science, technology and engineering, and helps make NASA's mission legacy more engaging to students, educators and the general public. We hope it inspires people to look beyond the headline discoveries and appreciate the engineering, experimentation and human ingenuity behind them. Factors considered during development We considered historical accuracy, scientific reliability, ease of navigation, accessibility, visual appeal and user engagement. We also paid attention to the differences between equipment that has completed its mission, equipment that has lost communication and spacecraft that remain active, so that the stories are engaging without misrepresenting their histories. Ultimately, we wanted to build something that doesn't just tell people what was left behind, but helps them understand why it matters.
